title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki: The Decision That Changed the World
alt_titles: Why Hiroshima? How the Target Was Chosen
The City Saved by a Cloud: Kokura and Nagasaki
description_summary: On 6 and 9 August 1945, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. This is the story of how the bombs were built, why those cities were chosen, how Japan surrendered, and why historians still argue about the decision.

scenes.narration: At 8.15 in the morning on 6 August 1945, an American B-29 bomber named Enola Gay flew over the Japanese city of Hiroshima. It was a clear summer day, and the city had been largely spared the heavy air raids that had burned much of Japan. People were walking to work and school. The crew released a single bomb, and the age of nuclear weapons began.

Three days later, a second bomb fell on Nagasaki. Within weeks, Japan had surrendered and the Second World War was over. This is the story of how those two bombs were built and why those two cities were chosen. It is also the story of a decision that historians still argue about, more than eighty years later.

shots.caption: The cloud over Hiroshima, 6 August 1945
The cloud over Nagasaki, 9 August 1945

card.label: atomic bombs ever used in war

scenes.narration: The story starts with a scientific discovery. In 1938, scientists in Germany split the uranium atom. Within months, laboratories in several countries had repeated the experiment. Physicists soon realised that a chain reaction could release enormous energy. Many feared Nazi Germany would build a bomb first.

stick.label: What if Germany builds it first?

scenes.narration: In 1939, Albert Einstein signed a letter warning President Franklin Roosevelt of the danger. After the United States entered the war, the effort became a vast secret programme, the Manhattan Project. Its scientific laboratory at Los Alamos, New Mexico, was led by the physicist Robert Oppenheimer.

shots.file: File:Trinity Test - Oppenheimer and Groves at Ground Zero 001.jpg
shots.caption: Oppenheimer and General Groves at the Trinity test site, 1945

scenes.narration: By 1945, the project employed many thousands of people in secret sites across America. President Truman later said it had cost two billion dollars, which he called the greatest scientific gamble in history. Germany surrendered in May 1945, before any bomb was ready. Japan fought on.

card.text: The greatest scientific gamble in history.

shots.file: File:The gadget in the Trinity Test Site tower (1945).jpg
shots.caption: The first test device in its tower, 1945

scenes.narration: On 16 July 1945, the first atomic bomb was tested in the New Mexico desert. It was code named Trinity. The flash lit up the mountains for miles. The weapon worked. Ten days later, the Allies issued a final warning to Japan.

shots.caption: The Trinity fireball, 16 milliseconds after detonation
The Trinity cloud, 12 seconds after detonation

scenes.narration: The work was spread across the country. Huge plants at Oak Ridge in Tennessee produced enriched uranium. Reactors at Hanford in Washington State made plutonium. The bombs themselves were designed at Los Alamos. Most of the people who worked there had no idea what they were building.

On 26 July, the Potsdam Declaration called on Japan to surrender unconditionally. The alternative, it said, was prompt and utter destruction. It did not mention the new weapon. Japan's government did not accept the terms.

shots.file: File:Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and President Truman (Potsdam Conference, July 1945).jpg
shots.caption: Stalin, Churchill and Truman at Potsdam, July 1945

card.text: The alternative for Japan is prompt and utter destruction.

scenes.narration: The man who would decide had only known about the bomb for a few months. Harry Truman became president when Franklin Roosevelt died in April 1945. Only after that was he fully briefed on the Manhattan Project, by Secretary of War Henry Stimson.

By then, American planners had already drawn up a list of target cities. It included Kokura, Hiroshima, Niigata and, at first, Kyoto. Secretary of War Henry Stimson had Kyoto removed because of its cultural importance. Nagasaki was added in its place.

card.label: added to the list on 25 July

scenes.narration: Hiroshima was chosen partly because it held a major army headquarters, and partly because its compact centre would show the bomb's power clearly. Some scientists had proposed a demonstration over an empty area instead. The idea was rejected, partly from doubt that it would make Japan surrender.

shots.caption: Hiroshima Castle, before the bombing
A model of central Hiroshima before 1945

scenes.narration: Enola Gay took off from the island of Tinian in the Pacific in the early hours of 6 August. Its pilot was Colonel Paul Tibbets. The bomb on board was called Little Boy. It used uranium, and no bomb of its design had ever been tested.

shots.file: File:Boeing B-29 Superfortress Enola Gay, 509th Composite Group, Dropped Atom Bomb on Hiroshima, Aug. 6, 1945 (10438069846).jpg
shots.caption: The B-29 Enola Gay
Members of the Enola Gay's crew

scenes.narration: At 8.15, the bomb fell for about forty five seconds. It exploded nearly 600 metres above the city. Its force was equal to about fifteen thousand tons of TNT. Much of the city centre was destroyed in an instant, and fires spread across what remained.

card.label: of TNT: Little Boy's explosive force

shots.file: File:Atomic cloud over Hiroshima - NARA 542192 - Edit.jpg
shots.caption: The cloud rising over Hiroshima

shots.file: File:Aerial view of Hiroshima Bomb Damage.jpg
shots.caption: Central Hiroshima after the bombing

scenes.narration: Exactly how many people died will never be known. Estimates for Hiroshima by the end of 1945 range from about 90,000 to 166,000. Many died in the first moment. Many more died in the following weeks from burns and radiation sickness. Most of them were civilians.

card.label: estimated deaths in Hiroshima by end of 1945

shots.caption: The dome that survived near the centre of the blast

scenes.narration: Sixteen hours later, President Truman announced the attack to the world. He called the weapon an atomic bomb. He warned that if Japan's leaders did not accept the terms, they could expect a rain of ruin from the air. Japan's leaders were still divided.

shots.caption: President Harry Truman

card.text: They may expect a rain of ruin from the air, the like of which has never been seen on this earth.

scenes.narration: Then came another blow. Earlier in the year, at Yalta, Stalin had promised his allies that the Soviet Union would join the war against Japan. On 8 August, the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and attacked Japanese forces in Manchuria. Japan had hoped the Soviets might help negotiate an end to the war. That hope was gone.

stick.label: 8 August: the Soviet Union declares war

card.label: Soviet Union declares war on Japan

scenes.narration: On the morning of 9 August, a second B-29, named Bockscar, flew towards its first target, the city of Kokura. Its pilot was Major Charles Sweeney. Clouds and drifting smoke covered Kokura. After three runs over the city, the crew could not see their aiming point. In Japan, escaping a disaster without ever knowing it is still sometimes called Kokura's luck.

card.label: bomb runs over Kokura
card.note: No clear view of the target

scenes.narration: Running low on fuel, Sweeney turned towards the secondary target, Nagasaki. At 11.02, the second bomb, called Fat Man, exploded over the city. It used plutonium and was even more powerful than the first. Nagasaki was also partly covered by cloud, and the bomb exploded over the Urakami valley, a few kilometres from the planned aiming point. The hills around Nagasaki contained some of the damage.

shots.file: File:Atomic cloud over Nagasaki from B-29.jpg
shots.caption: The cloud over Nagasaki, seen from a B-29

scenes.narration: A report by the city in 1950 estimated that about 74,000 people in Nagasaki had died by the end of 1945. Other estimates range from about 60,000 to 80,000. Kokura, saved by the weather, has never forgotten how close it came.

card.label: estimated deaths in Nagasaki by end of 1945

shots.file: File:Nuclear mushroom cloud of Fat Man.jpg
shots.caption: The cloud from the Nagasaki bomb

scenes.narration: In Tokyo, Japan's leaders were deadlocked. Some wanted to fight on. Others wanted to accept the Allied terms. Emperor Hirohito broke the deadlock, telling them the war must end. Even then, a group of army officers tried to seize the palace and stop the surrender, and failed. On 10 August, Japan said it would accept the Potsdam terms, asking that the emperor's position be preserved.

shots.caption: Emperor Hirohito, 1945

card.label: Japan offers to accept the terms
card.note: With a condition on the emperor

scenes.narration: On 15 August, the Japanese people heard their emperor's voice on the radio for the first time. In a recorded message, he announced that Japan would accept the Allied terms. He referred to a new and most cruel bomb. The formal surrender was signed aboard the battleship USS Missouri on 2 September.

shots.caption: Japan's formal surrender aboard USS Missouri, 2 September 1945

shots.file: File:Mamoru Shigemitsu signs the Instrument of Surrender, officially ending the Second World War.jpg
shots.caption: Japan's foreign minister signs the surrender

scenes.narration: The surrender ended the deadliest war in history. But the decision to use the bombs has been argued over ever since. Supporters say the bombs shortened the war and saved more lives than they took. An invasion of Japan was planned for November 1945, and both sides expected enormous losses. How many would have died is itself disputed: wartime estimates varied enormously.

Critics say Japan was already close to defeat, and that targeting cities full of civilians was morally wrong, some say a war crime. Some historians, including Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, argue that the Soviet declaration of war did more to force Japan's surrender than the bombs did. The debate is still unresolved.

The survivors are known in Japan as hibakusha, meaning people affected by the bombs. The Japanese government has recognised about 650,000 of them. As of March 2025, about 99,000 were still alive. Many suffered illnesses linked to radiation for decades, and some faced discrimination at work and in marriage. Many spent their lives warning the world about nuclear weapons.

shots.caption: The Children's Peace Monument, Hiroshima
The Peace Bell in Hiroshima

scenes.narration: In 2024, Nihon Hidankyo, an organisation of survivors, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for that work. The ruined dome near the centre of the Hiroshima blast was kept as it stood. In 1996, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

shots.caption: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial today

card.label: Nobel Peace Prize for Nihon Hidankyo

shots.file: File:20190202 Nagasaki Peace Park Maiden of Peace-1.jpg
shots.caption: Nagasaki Peace Park

scenes.narration: In the eighty years since, nuclear weapons have been built in their thousands, but never again used in war. Hiroshima and Nagasaki remain the only cities to have suffered an atomic attack. Every August, both cities ring bells and ask the world to keep it that way.
